title: The Art of Remembering Answers
description: Discover why caching is the single biggest performance win in system design, and learn the patterns that power every fast application.

segments.text: Imagine you're in a library. Every time someone asks you a question, you walk to the back, find the book, read the answer, and walk back. Now imagine a hundred people asking the same question. That's your database without caching.
Here's what it looks like. Client sends a request, server asks the database, database grinds through disk reads, and eventually returns the result. Two hundred milliseconds. Every. Single. Time.
And the worst part? Most of those queries return the exact same data. The homepage, the product list, the user profile — same answers, queried thousands of times. What a waste.
What if we just... remembered the answer? Store the result in fast memory, and the next time someone asks, hand it over instantly. That's a cache. It's that simple — and that powerful.
Watch this. Same request comes in, but now the server checks the cache first. Boom — data's right there in memory. Two milliseconds instead of two hundred. That's a hundred times faster!

But what about the first time, when the answer isn't cached yet? That's a cache miss. The server checks the cache, finds nothing, goes to the database, gets the answer, and stores it in the cache for next time.
Here's a question for you to chew on. If you cache data, how long should you keep it? Forever?
segments.thought_prompt: What could go wrong if cached data never expires?

segments.text: If you cache forever, the data goes stale. A user changes their name but the old name keeps showing up. That's why we use TTL — time to live. After, say, sixty seconds, the cached entry expires and the next request fetches fresh data.

Now let me show you the most common pattern — cache-aside. The application owns the logic: check cache first, if miss then query database, then write the result back to cache. Simple, flexible, and used everywhere.

Alternative pattern: write-through. Every time you write to the database, you also write to the cache immediately. The cache is always warm and fresh. Trade-off? Every write is a little slower because you're updating two places.
There's a famous saying in computer science: there are only two hard things — naming things and cache invalidation. Let me show you why.
segments.thought_prompt: When data changes, how do you make sure ALL caches everywhere have the correct version?

segments.text: Knowing when to expire, update, or delete cached data is genuinely hard at scale. But the fundamentals you just learned — hits, misses, TTL, cache-aside, write-through — that's your foundation. Next up, we'll tackle eviction policies and cache stampedes.
